A garland is a decorative strand or loop made by weaving, threading, or linking together flowers, leaves, greenery, or other ornamental items. Think of it as a flexible "chain of beauty" — a connected arrangement of things designed to adorn a place, an object, or a person.

A garland takes one of two physical forms. The first is a long, flowing strand — like a rope of flowers or pine branches that drapes and bends naturally. The second is a circular ring or loop — like a crown of flowers for the head, or a ring of greenery hung on a door.

The single most important quality of a garland is its flexibility. Because it bends and curves, it can be draped over a fireplace mantel, wound around a pillar, hung in a sweeping arc between two points, or worn on the head or around the neck. This is what makes a garland so versatile as a decoration.

Traditional garlands are made from natural materials: fresh or dried flowers, leaves, vines, evergreen branches (such as pine, ivy, or holly), and berries. However, the word extends comfortably to non-natural materials too. Tinsel garlands (shiny metallic strands), light garlands (strings of fairy lights looped decoratively), bead garlands, fabric garlands, and paper garlands are all perfectly valid uses of the word. The common thread is always the same: items linked together into a strand or ring, purely for decoration.
Where and when you encounter garlands

Garlands appear across many cultures and occasions, which is what makes knowing this word so useful.

During festivals and holidays, garlands are among the most common decorations. At Christmas, pine or holly garlands are draped along staircase railings, hung over fireplaces, and framed around doorways. Tinsel garlands and light garlands adorn Christmas trees.

In many weddings and ceremonies, garlands of flowers decorate venues, arches, and tables. In South and Southeast Asian weddings, the exchange of flower garlands between the bride and groom is often a central, sacred moment of the ceremony itself.

In many cultures — particularly across South Asia — placing a fresh flower garland around the neck of an honored guest is one of the warmest gestures of welcome and respect. This is closely related in spirit to the Hawaiian lei, which is essentially a flower garland worn around the neck.

In religious practice, garlands of flowers are offered to deities in Hindu temples and are used to decorate altars, statues, and sacred spaces in many traditions around the world.

At funerals and memorials, garlands of flowers are placed on coffins, graves, and monuments as a mark of respect and remembrance.

In ancient Greece and Rome, garlands of laurel leaves were placed on the heads of victorious athletes, scholars, and military heroes — a crown of glory and honor. This is the origin of the familiar image of a "laurel wreath."
A less common but real meaning

The word garland can also be used figuratively to mean a collection or anthology, especially of literary or musical works. If someone publishes a "garland of poems," it means a gathered, curated collection of poems — the idea being that just as a garland strings individual flowers together into something beautiful, an anthology strings individual works together into a unified whole. You may encounter this meaning in older books or formal writing.
How a garland differs from similar things

A wreath is always a closed circle — a ring shape — and is typically hung on a door or wall. A garland can be either a long strand or a circular loop, so the two words overlap. In everyday usage, though, when people say "garland" they almost always mean the long, draping strand. When they mean the ring, they usually just say "wreath."

A lei is the Hawaiian term for a flower garland worn around the neck. The two objects are essentially the same thing; "lei" simply belongs to Hawaiian tradition and language.

"She wove a garland of wildflowers and wore it in her hair."

"A garland of pine branches and red berries was draped along the staircase for the holidays."

"The temple entrance was hung with long garlands of orange marigolds."

"He strung a garland of fairy lights across the ceiling, giving the room a warm, festive glow."

"In ancient times, champions were crowned with a garland of laurel leaves as a symbol of their achievement."

"The editor published a garland of short stories from writers across the country."
